docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
An experiment is a real task image run against a real Postgres database with dummy data, on the development node. Its dataset's credentials go through nexus-api's secret, and its results are delivered to Gitea, so it exercises the whole path. This page is for people developing analytics images or the node itself. For a real node, see Set up a project.

The experiments' databases are their own Helm release in the experiments namespace, apart from the FN chart. The node only sees the dataset that fncli registers, at db-datasets.experiments.svc. You need the development cluster running (Run locally).

docs.title: What is in an experiment
docs.text:
Everything an experiment needs lives in one folder, experiments/<name>/:

File What it is values.yaml The experiment's entry for the databases chart: it makes the database, the role and a generated password secret (db-datasets-<name>, with username and password) dataset.yaml A node file with only the dataset and its secret, read from the chart's secret. No project, no repositories seed.sh, seed/ Prints the SQL that fills the database. Must be safe to rerun docker-bake.hcl, image/ The task image's source and its build target, <name>-fn trigger.json The trigger file run sends: the image, and whatever else the task is asked for (CPU and memory limits, say) project.env Settings of run only: RUN_TIMEOUT

The project and its repositories stay in node files under bootstrap/examples/ (globals-<name>.yaml and projects/<name>.yaml), which assign the dataset by name.

demo is the smallest experiment: a database demo-db with a role demo_user, a tiny cdm.person table and an empty results schema, and a task image demo-fn that writes mock results. It has no project of its own: the demo node files hold the repositories and the project.

docs.title: Run an experiment
docs.text:
fncli experiment deploy                    # install the databases release (safe to rerun)
fncli experiment build NAME            # build and push the task image
fncli experiment seed NAME             # load the dummy data
fncli experiment setup NAME            # check the names, register the dataset, then the repositories and project
fncli experiment run NAME              # trigger a pull request, follow the task to the results pull request

They are safe to rerun after a failure. setup, run, teardown and down talk to the node, so they need your context file (Using fncli). If fncli experiment says "No such command", run mise run setup in this checkout.

setup first checks that dataset.yaml names what the chart makes: its dataset is dbs.<name>.name of values.yaml, and its secret reads the Kubernetes secret dbs.<name>.secret.name in experiments. A name that does not match fails here, before the node gets a dataset it cannot use. Then it applies dataset.yaml, and the experiment's globals and project files if it has them.

run takes its pull request's project and repositories from the project file and the node, and the task's image from trigger.json. It adds DEV_ENV from your shell (JSON) to the task's env, which is how a quick run is asked for (DEV_ENV='{"SOME_FLAG": "1"}' fncli experiment run NAME). FULL=1 leaves it out.

To run just the image, against the database and with no node:

fncli experiment run NAME --local

It needs fncli directly. The results land under experiments/results/NAME/.

docs.title: Add an experiment
docs.text:
1. Put the image's source in experiments/sources/NAME (or in experiments/NAME/image/). The image reads the task contract (Analytics container development): CONNECTION_STRING, CDM_SCHEMA, WRITE_SCHEMA, and it writes to ARTIFACT_PATH.
  2. Copy an existing experiment folder to NAME, and change the names and the seed: values.yaml (dbs.NAME), dataset.yaml (the dataset and secret must match it), trigger.json (the image), project.env, and copies of the globals and project node files for the repositories and the project.
  3. Run fncli experiment deploy. It upgrades the release with the new database, so it works on a running cluster. Then build, seed, setup and run.

A dataset name is unique across the node, so two experiments cannot share one. A node file whose project names a dataset that is not on the node is blocked, so setup the experiment before applying its project.

docs.title: Building images
docs.text:
Images are built with docker buildx bake. The repo's root docker-bake.hcl holds the node's own images, and each experiment brings its own docker-bake.hcl with one target, <name>-fn, found automatically. An experiment whose source is not there (cloned separately) is skipped.

Command What it does mise run images Build and push the node's images and every experiment's target to the local registry mise run image --target <target> One target mise run image-reload --target <target> Push one target, then roll the deployments mise run images-release --tag <tag> The release group, loaded into your local Docker, not pushed fncli experiment build NAME Build and push just one experiment's image

Dev images are tagged latest. mise run deploy builds the default group for you.

docs.title: Check task isolation
docs.text:
attacker is a hostile task image, not an experiment. It tries to read other runs' folders, plant symbolic links and ../ paths in its output, reach nexus-api, Gitea and the Kubernetes API, read a service account token or another task's secret, and keep privileges. Each attempt prints BLOCKED or LEAKED, and the PLANTED lines are judged by what delivery does with them.

Run it like any experiment (up, build attacker, seed attacker, setup attacker, run attacker), then read attack-report.txt in the delivered results.zip, and check the zip holds no symbolic link or file from outside the run's folder. See Architecture for what is being tested.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
• fncli experiment teardown NAME removes what setup registered in the node for NAME: its project and repositories (if it has node files), then its dataset and secret. The release and its database stay. The backend refuses to delete a dataset that another project still uses.
  • fncli experiment down does that for every experiment, then uninstalls the release. The secrets and database files stay, so a later setup gets the same data back. If a demo project still uses demo-db, it stops: delete the demo project first.
  • To start from empty: kubectl delete ns experiments, then delete ~/.fn/data/experiments. Postgres owns it, so that needs root or the kind node.

The repo's experiments/README.md is the source for this page.

docs.title: Federated Node - Documentation
docs.text:
2.x beta. This documentation covers the 2.x Federated Node, which is in beta.

This documentation covers deploying, setting up, testing, and using the PHEMS Federated Node (FN) 2.x.

docs.title: What is the Federated Node?
docs.text:
The Federated Node lets researchers run analytical tasks against sensitive datasets without the data ever leaving your institution. Analytics code (packaged as a Docker container) is sent to the data - not the other way around. Only the results come out, as a pull request that someone at your institution reviews before it is merged.

It deploys as a Helm chart onto a Kubernetes cluster. Tasks are asked for with a pull request, so nothing has to call into your node to start one.

Core components bundled in the chart:

  • nexus-api - the FN API (FastAPI). It keeps the record of everything and decides what is allowed
  • Dagster - polls the git repositories, starts task pods, and delivers results
  • Keycloak - logins and the admin role
  • Traefik - reverse proxy and ingress (recommended for production)
  • PostgreSQL - FN metadata (projects, tasks, results) - you provide this externally in production

You also need a git host for the trigger and results repositories: GitHub (with a GitHub App) or Gitea. The chart can run a Gitea for development only.

docs.title: How a task runs
docs.text:
1. A researcher adds a small JSON file (the task spec: which image to run, which dataset) to the project's trigger repository, in a pull request.
  2. Someone at the institution merges it.
  3. The node sees the merged pull request, turns it into a task, and starts a pod in your cluster with the researcher's image, next to the dataset.
  4. When the task finishes, the node pushes the result files to the project's results repository as a branch and opens a pull request.
  5. Someone at the institution reviews that pull request. Merging it is the release of the results.

Architecture explains each part. Researcher guide shows the researcher's side.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Understanding how it fits together: Architecture covers the components, the flow, and the decisions you need to make yourself before production.

Trying it on your own machine first: Run locally takes a Linux or WSL2 machine from nothing to a working demo, on a local cluster with a Gitea inside it.

Deploying for the first time: Prerequisites, then Deploy: Core with the guide for your platform, then Post-deploy testing. The platform guides are Azure (AKS), AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and On-Premises.

Setting up a project for researchers: Set up a project covers the git provider, repositories, dataset and project, in the order they have to be made.

Running tasks as a researcher: Researcher guide.

Building an analytics container: Analytics container development covers the environment variables, where to write results, and what the pod is and is not allowed to do.

Registering the databases tasks read from: Datasets.

Developing against the node: Using fncli and Experiments.

Looking after a running node: Operations.

What changed in each release is in the release notes.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: How to look after a running Federated Node 2.x: start the sensors, switch things on and off, check that it is healthy, and work out why a pull request did nothing.

docs.title: Start the sensors
docs.text:
Every Dagster sensor starts stopped, so nothing is polled and no task runs until you start them. Do it once the first project is enabled. The order does not matter, and after a reinstall you start them again.

With the API (admin):

curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "RUNNING"}' | jq
curl -sS "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq        # every sensor, its status and latest tick

With the Dagster UI. It has no login, so reach it by port-forward and never publish it:

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node svc/federatednode-dagster-webserver 3000:80

Open http://localhost:3000, go to Automation, and turn on all twelve sensors.

The sensors, by group:

Group Sensors Job ingest git_pull_request_ingest_sensor Polls each trigger repository once and stores new merged pull requests evaluate git_pull_request_evaluate_sensor Turns each stored pull request into a task, or rejects it with a cause launcher task_launcher_sensor Starts a Dagster run for each pending task status five run-status sensors, task_reconcile_sensor Copy the run's status onto the task delivery task_results_delivery_sensor, results_pull_request_sync_sensor, results_delivery_retry_sensor Push results, track the results pull request, retry failures

How often they tick is the chart value fnDagster.sensors.minIntervalSeconds (30 seconds by default), and how long a failed run waits before a retry is retryIntervalSeconds (60 seconds). To pause the node, stop the sensors the same way, with {"status": "STOPPED"}.

docs.title: Switch things on and off
docs.text:
Two flags sit on every resource. Enabled is a switch anyone allowed to manage the resource can flip. Revoked is admin only and takes effect at once. A resource is active only when it is enabled and not revoked, and only active ones are used.

To stop Do this A whole project PATCH /projects/<id> with {"enabled": false}, or {"revoked": true} (admin) One project's use of one resource PATCH the assignment: /projects/<id>/datasets/<dataset_id>, /projects/<id>/repositories/triggers/<id>, /projects/<id>/repositories/results/<id> A resource for every project PATCH /global/datasets/<id>, /global/repositories/triggers/<id>, /global/repositories/results/<id> or /global/providers/<id> with enabled or revoked A credential PATCH /global/secrets/<label>. Disabling it also disables the datasets and repositories that use it, and moves its value to the quarantine namespace. They stay off when you turn the secret back on

What happens to work in flight:

  • The launcher fails a pending task, with the cause in its state_cause, when anything it uses is revoked or deleted.
  • A result for a revoked or deleted results repository is recorded as REVOKED and nothing is delivered.
  • A result for a disabled one is retried once it is switched back on.

DELETE is a soft delete: the record leaves the API, its assignments go with it, and the name is free again. Deleting a dataset or repository that projects still use is a 409 listing them. The full table of what each state does is in the repo's revoke-and-enabled.md.

docs.title: Checking on it
docs.text: Question Where to look Can everything be reached? GET /global/healthcheck, GET /projects/<id>/healthcheck, and per resource GET /global/datasets/<id>/healthcheck, /global/secrets/<label>/healthcheck, /global/providers/<id>/healthcheck, /global/repositories/triggers/<id>/healthcheck, /global/repositories/results/<id>/healthcheck What is this project doing? GET /projects/<id>/tasks Is a run stuck or failing? The Dagster UI, Runs, for the logs of each step Are the sensors running? GET /dagster/sensors, or the Dagster UI Automation page Whole-node checklist The repo's deploy and health checklist

docs.title: Reading a run
docs.text: Open the Dagster UI by port-forward (above), and go to Runs. A task's run is tagged with the task's id. Its logs show each step, including whatever the container wrote to stdout and stderr.

docs.title: A pull request was merged and nothing happened
docs.text: Cause How you see it Sensors are stopped (the default) GET /dagster/sensors: STOPPED The project is disabled, or an assignment is inactive The project or assignment shows enabled false or revoked true The pull request does not add a .json file under watch_dir, or targets another branch No trigger is made for that project (it is skipped and logged) It was merged before the trigger repository was assigned or the project enabled Skipped by design. Enable with backfill, or merge a new one It adds more than one spec file, or the spec is not valid The trigger is REJECTED and state_cause says why A token is wrong or expired The resource's healthcheck fails and names it. Rotate it with PATCH /global/secrets/<label> The task stays pending state_cause on the task: usually the dataset assignment is inactive or its secret is disabled. Fix the cause, then POST /projects/<id>/tasks/<task_id>/retry The task starts but its container cannot reach the database The container times out connecting. The database is not in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress (Deploy: Core)

docs.title: Results not delivered
docs.text: A succeeded task whose results do not appear: check the task's results (GET /projects/<id>/tasks/<task_id>/results). A failed delivery shows its error and is retried by the delivery sensors. The usual causes are a results zip over 10 MiB (fnDagster.results.maxZipBytes) and a token without write access to the results repository. A task that failed delivers nothing.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The per-run folders on the shared results volume are not removed after delivery. Watch the volume's size.
  • A result over the size cap has no other route: it fails.
  • The Dagster UI has no login. Reach it only by port-forward.

The repo's known issues list the details.

docs.title: Post-Deploy Testing
docs.text: Use this guide to verify your Federated Node 2.x is healthy before you set up a project and hand it over to users. It checks the install only.

docs.title: 1. Check pod status
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n federated-node
kubectl get pods -n keycloak
kubectl get jobs -A

Every pod should reach Running, and the *-db-init and keycloak-realm-init jobs should show Completed. The first start takes a few minutes while Keycloak and the databases initialise.

If anything is stuck, check its logs:

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n federated-node
kubectl logs <pod> -n federated-node

docs.title: 2. Set your hostname
docs.text:
All examples in this guide use $FN_HOST.

If accessing via a public hostname: 

export FN_HOST=https://fn.your-institution.example.com

If port-forwarding to nexus-api directly (no Traefik): 

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node service/nexus-api 5000:5000
export FN_HOST=http://localhost:5000

docs.title: 3. Health check
docs.text:
curl "$FN_HOST/health_check"

It returns "status": "ok" when nexus-api can reach Keycloak, and a 502 otherwise. If it stays at 502, give Keycloak a minute and retry, then check the Keycloak pod's logs.

docs.title: 4. Login
docs.text:
Log in as the first user, with the email from firstUserSecret.email and the password in the secret you created for it. /login takes form fields, not JSON, and returns a bearer token:

PASSWORD=$(kubectl get secret -n federated-node fn-first-user -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d)

TOKEN=$(curl --silent "$FN_HOST/login" \
    -F "username=admin@your-institution.example.com" \
    -F "password=$PASSWORD" | jq -r '.token')

The token lasts 8 hours (POST /refresh_token renews it). The Keycloak admin password, if you need it, is in the kc-secrets secret in the keycloak namespace.

Then check the node as a whole:

curl -sS "$FN_HOST/global/healthcheck" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq

A failing check shows in the body with a status of 200, never a 500, and never contains a secret value. On a new node with nothing registered yet, it has little to check.

docs.title: 5. Check Dagster
docs.text:
The Dagster UI has no login and no route, so reach it with a port-forward. It listens on port 80, so 3000:3000 fails:

kubectl port-forward -n federated-node svc/federatednode-dagster-webserver 3000:80

Open http://localhost:3000 and check that the code location loads with no error. Under Automation you should see twelve sensors, all stopped. That is how a new node starts.

docs.title: 6. Register a test dataset
docs.text:
A dataset registration tells the node where a research database lives. The node stores the connection details and never copies the data. This step proves the node can reach a database from inside the cluster. Use a database you have, with a login that can read it. The full list of fields and types is in Datasets.

Store the login as a secret (the keys are USERNAME and PASSWORD), then register the dataset:

AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json")

curl -sS -X POST "$FN_HOST/global/secrets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "label": "test-dataset-creds",
  "provider": "K8S",
  "values": {"USERNAME": "db-user", "PASSWORD": "db-password"}
}' | jq

DATASET_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN_HOST/global/datasets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "name": "test_dataset",
  "host": "your-database-host.example.com",
  "port": 5432,
  "type": "postgres",
  "secret_label": "test-dataset-creds",
  "read_schema": "public"
}' | jq -r '.id')

curl -sS "$FN_HOST/global/datasets/$DATASET_ID/healthcheck" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

The healthcheck connects to the database with the stored login. A failure is reported in the body, with a status of 200. If it fails, the message says why: a wrong host or port, a wrong login, or a cluster firewall in between. The healthcheck covers PostgreSQL and SQL Server datasets.

If you registered a throwaway dataset, remove it so the name is free: DELETE /global/datasets/$DATASET_ID, and then DELETE /global/secrets/test-dataset-creds?force=true. Without force the secret is refused while an enabled dataset still uses it.

Whether a task can reach the database is a separate question, because task pods are limited by the network policy. A database on a private address works by default. For any other address, list it in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress (Deploy: Core).

docs.title: 7. Run the chart's own tests
docs.text:
helm test federatednode -n federated-node --logs

With smoketests: true in your values, the tests also create and delete real rows. The full list of checks for a node is the repo's deploy and health checklist.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Datasets: register the databases tasks will read from.
  • Set up a project: its repositories, its dataset, and the sensors. The repo's MANAGEMENT.md walks through it.
  • Researcher guide: how a researcher asks for a task, once the project is enabled.
  • Operations: looking after a running node.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before deploying the Federated Node 2.x, make sure the following are in place.

docs.title: Required tools
docs.text:
Tool Purpose Install guide kubectl Interact with your Kubernetes cluster docs.kubernetes.io helm (v3+) Deploy the FN chart helm.sh/docs/intro/install jq Parse API responses in shell examples stedolan.github.io/jq

An example values.yaml is in Deploy: Core, and the platform guides add the storage, ingress and certificate settings for each platform.

docs.title: Kubernetes cluster
docs.text:
Any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster works. Each platform has its own guide with its prerequisites and known issues:

  • Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
  • AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)
  • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
  • On-premises (RKE2, k3s, kubeadm)

Size the cluster for the base pods plus your analytics task pods. Start with 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM per node. A task pod gets 500m CPU and 1 GiB of memory by default and may use up to 2 CPU and 4 GiB, and a task spec may ask for up to 4 CPU and 16 GiB. These are taskCompute.default and taskCompute.max, so size your nodes for the number of tasks you expect to run at once.

The cluster's network plugin (CNI) must enforce NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, or your cloud's network policy add-on. The chart denies a task pod all traffic except cluster DNS, the private address ranges in taskNetworkPolicy.privateEgress and the dataset databases you list in taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress. On a CNI that ignores NetworkPolicy, that rule does nothing.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
The FN needs a PostgreSQL server that the cluster can reach, with an admin login. It needs its own databases on it (fn_nexus for nexus-api, keycloak_db and dagster), not your research data. By default the chart creates them and their roles for you, and nexus-api creates its tables on first start.

Have ready the hostname, the port, and the admin login and password. On a managed service (Azure, RDS, Cloud SQL) the admin is not called postgres: you set it in db.superuser. If the server requires TLS, set db.enforceSSL.

If a DBA owns the databases and you have no admin login, the chart can instead use roles and databases that already exist. Deploy: Core covers both.

Back up Keycloak's database as well as nexus-api's. They are separate databases on the same server. Restoring only nexus-api's gives you a node that knows its datasets and projects but has lost every login.

docs.title: Shared storage
docs.text:
Task pods and Dagster's run pods write results to the same volume, so it must be ReadWriteMany. ReadWriteOnce disks do not work. Supported backends:

  • Azure Files - for AKS
  • AWS EFS - for EKS (the EFS CSI driver and an access point are needed)
  • NFS - cloud-agnostic, on-prem friendly. On GKE, use Filestore
  • Local host path - single node and development only

The choice is made at install time and is awkward to change later, because it means recreating the volumes. The per-run result folders are not removed after delivery, so size the volume for the output of every run you expect to keep.

docs.title: A hostname and a certificate
docs.text: The node needs a DNS name pointing at Traefik, and a TLS certificate for it. Either create the certificate yourself, or have cert-manager get and renew one. The chart's own cert-manager issuer covers Azure DNS and Route 53. Your platform guide says what to do elsewhere.

docs.title: A git host and two repositories
docs.text:
Tasks are asked for through git, so every project needs a trigger repository and a results repository. They can be the same repository, as long as the directories used for each do not overlap. They must already exist: the node does not create them. Use either:

  • GitHub, with a GitHub App installed on the repositories (read and write on Contents and Pull requests).
  • Gitea, with an OAuth2 application for the admin user.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Outbound HTTPS to ghcr.io (images), to your git host (api.github.com for GitHub), and to wherever your analytics images live. If the cluster has no internet egress, mirror the FN images and your analytics images into an internal registry.

Nothing needs to call into the node to start a task. Admins who use the API reach nexus-api over HTTPS through Traefik, so one address must be reachable from their workstations or VPN.

docs.title: Install the Gateway API and Traefik CRDs
docs.text:
If you use the chart's Traefik (traefik.enabled: true, recommended for production), two sets of Kubernetes CRDs must exist before helm install. The chart refuses to install without them, and says so. This is a one-time step per cluster. From a checkout of the repository:

./scripts/gateway-api-installer.sh

It applies the Gateway API CRDs (version 1.4.0 unless you pass another) and the Traefik CRDs, with server-side apply. Skip this only if you set traefik.enabled: false and bring your own ingress.

docs.title: Notes on secrets
docs.text:
Credentials are Kubernetes secrets, not values in your values.yaml. The chart creates most of them (database passwords, Keycloak credentials, the Dagster login). Deploy: Core lists the few you have to create.

A few characters cause problems in shell --from-literal commands: " must be escaped as \", and % needs special handling. When in doubt, use a YAML manifest and pre-encode the value with echo -n "yourvalue" | base64.

Create the namespace before the secrets. Secrets created in the wrong namespace are not visible to the FN pods:

kubectl create namespace federated-node

Git and dataset credentials are not Helm secrets. You register them through the API after the install, as global secrets.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
Follow Deploy: Core, which covers the steps common to every platform, and add the guide for your platform alongside it:

  • Deploy: Azure (AKS)
  • Deploy: AWS (EKS)
  • Deploy: GCP (GKE)
  • Deploy: On-Premises

docs.title: Researcher Guide
docs.text:
This guide is for researchers who want to run an analysis on a Federated Node 2.x. You do not call the node to start a task. You write a small JSON file, add it to the project's trigger repository in a pull request, and when someone at the institution merges it, the node runs your container next to the data. The results come back as another pull request.

Before you start, ask the node's admin for:

  • the trigger repository, its watch directory and its base branch (where your spec file goes);
  • the name of the dataset you may use, or whether the project has a default;
  • where the results repository is, so you can find your results.

You also need a container image that follows the container contract, pushed somewhere the cluster can pull it from.

docs.title: 1. Write the task spec
docs.text:
The spec file says what to run. Only spec and metadata are allowed at the top level, and spec is required:

{
  "spec": {
    "image": "ghcr.io/your-org/your-analytics-image:1.0",
    "dataset": "my-dataset",
    "env": {"COHORT": "paediatric", "MIN_AGE": "0"},
    "tags": {"team": "analytics"},
    "config": {"epochs": 3},
    "compute": {
      "requests": {"cpu": "500m", "memory": "1Gi"},
      "limits": {"cpu": "2", "memory": "4Gi"}
    }
  },
  "metadata": {"ticket": "ABC-1"}
}
Field Required What it does spec.image yes The container image to run, up to 256 characters. spec.dataset no The name of a dataset your project has and that is switched on. Without it, the project's default dataset is used, if it has one. spec.env no Environment variables for your container. See below. spec.tags no Text labels copied onto the task's run. spec.config no A JSON object your container reads as a file, at the path in CONFIG_PATH. Its contents are not checked. spec.compute no The CPU and memory to ask for: requests and limits, each with an optional cpu and memory. metadata no Yours: any JSON, not checked, kept with the task and delivered with the results.

Any other field, at either level, makes the pull request REJECTED.

env:

  • A name matches ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ and arrives upper-cased.
  • Values reach your container as text. Send strings: a JSON true arrives as True.
  • You cannot set ARTIFACT_PATH, CDM_SCHEMA, WRITE_SCHEMA, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, CONNECTION_STRING or CONFIG_PATH, or any name starting with DAGSTER_ or KUBERNETES_, in any letter case. The node sets those itself.
  • All of env, as JSON, is at most 32 KiB.

tags: a key is 1 to 63 letters, digits, _, . or - (so no /), and a value is text.

compute: values are Kubernetes quantities (500m, 2, 512Mi, 4Gi). A limit cannot be lower than its request, and nothing can be over the node's maximum. A request with no limit of its own cannot be over the node's default limit. Without compute, the node's defaults apply. Ask your admin for the numbers (taskCompute in the chart).

The whole file is at most 64 KiB. The exact rules are in the spec schema, which your editor can use to check the file.

docs.title: 2. Open and merge the pull request
docs.text:
1. In the trigger repository, on a branch, add the spec file under the watch directory, for example specs/first-task.json.
  2. Open a pull request into the base branch.
  3. Someone with merge rights merges it. Only merged pull requests are read.

What the node does with a merged pull request:

The pull request Result Adds exactly one .json file under the watch directory, with a valid spec A task is created Adds more than one .json file under the watch directory REJECTED: "Several new spec files" Adds one, but the spec is not valid REJECTED, with the reason Adds no .json file under the watch directory, or goes to another branch Ignored: no task, no error Was merged before your project was enabled Ignored, unless the admin asked for a backfill

Only added files count. Changing or deleting a spec file does nothing, and editing a spec after it is merged changes nothing: the task keeps the spec as read at the merge. To run again with changes, add a new file in a new pull request.

The task is named <project name>:PR#<pull request number>.

docs.title: 3. Wait for the task
docs.text:
The node checks for new pull requests every 30 seconds or so, then queues the task and starts a pod. The task goes through PENDING, QUEUED, RUNNING and then SUCCESS or FAILED (CANCELED if it is stopped). Your admin can see the run and its logs in Dagster, and can read the task through the API (GET /projects/<id>/tasks).

If nothing seems to happen after a few minutes, the usual causes are on the admin's side: the sensors are stopped, the project or one of its resources is switched off, or your pull request was one of the ignored kinds above. A rejected pull request or a task that cannot start has its reason in state_cause.

A task that fails delivers nothing. The container must exit with status 0 to succeed.

docs.title: 4. Get your results
docs.text:
When the task succeeds, the node pushes the results to the project's results repository and opens a results pull request from a new branch into the project's results base_branch. Under the project's target_dir, the branch and the files are laid out like this:

<target_dir>/<trigger repository name>/<pr number>/<task id>/
    results.zip     everything your container wrote to ARTIFACT_PATH
    spec.json       your spec file, byte for byte (so your metadata rides along)
    run.json        the node, project, trigger, task and delivery details

The branch is named <target_dir>/<trigger repository name>/<pr number>/<task id>-<merge commit sha, first 7>.

The results.zip can be at most 10 MiB (the node's setting fnDagster.results.maxZipBytes). Over that, the delivery fails. Symbolic links in your output are skipped. The structure of run.json is in the run schema.

The results pull request is the review step. Someone at the institution reads it, and merging it releases the results. Closing it without merging does not. The node records which happened.

The outcome is not commented back on your trigger pull request, so look in the results repository.

docs.title: Trying it
docs.text: On a development node, fncli trigger opens and merges the pull request for you. The spec file you give it is exactly the one described here.

docs.title: Run Locally
docs.text:
This guide takes a Linux or WSL2 machine with nothing installed, and a fresh clone of the repository, to a working Federated Node 2.x on a local cluster, and walks a pull request through it to a results pull request. You do it once against a Gitea that runs inside the cluster, and once against a GitHub repository and GitHub App of your own.

This is for trying and developing the FN. For a real cluster, use Prerequisites and Deploy: Core. The repo's FRESH_SETUP.md and DEMO.md are the sources for this page, and the repo wins where they differ.

docs.title: What you end up with
docs.text:
• A local kind cluster with the FN installed, and a Gitea running inside it.
  • A small demo database, registered with the node as a dataset.
  • fncli, a command-line tool, on your PATH. fncli apply sets a node up from files, and fncli demo walks one pull request through it, one confirmed step at a time: it opens and merges a pull request, waits for the task to run, and merges the results pull request. fncli delete cleans up. Using fncli explains the files.

docs.title: 1. Install the tools
docs.text:
Tool Why git, curl, jq clone, installers, scripts Docker builds the images, runs kind and the local registries. docker ps must work without sudo kubectl, helm (v3), kind the cluster and the chart tilt the port-forwards fncli needs, and live reload mise mise run setup installs Python 3.12 and fncli (step 4); it also runs the repo's mise run tasks gh (optional) gives fncli a GitHub token for the GitHub demo, if you do not set RESEARCHER_GIT_TOKEN

On Debian, Ubuntu or WSL:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git curl jq

Then mise, from its installer. Activate it in your shell, and open a new terminal:

curl https://mise.run | sh
echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc     # zsh: ~/.zshrc and `mise activate zsh`

Install the rest from their own guides: Docker, kubectl, helm, kind and Tilt. The repo pins only Helm v3 and Python 3.12; use current releases of the others.

Check that everything is on the PATH:

for t in git curl jq docker kubectl helm kind tilt mise; do command -v $t >/dev/null || echo "missing: $t"; done

docs.title: 2. Clone
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Aridhia-Open-Source/PHEMS_federated_node.git
cd PHEMS_federated_node
git checkout beta

Run every command from here on from the repo root, unless a step says otherwise.

One dev cluster has one owner at a time. To work in a second copy of the repo, tear the first down, or deploy with --force-owner. mise run worktree --name <dir> --branch <branch> makes a sibling copy with your local config files copied over.

docs.title: 3. Local config
docs.text:
Two files, both gitignored. Do this before the cluster step.

cp .dev.env.example .dev.env
cp k8s/federated-node/dev.example.values.yml k8s/federated-node/dev.values.yaml

In .dev.env, set:

Variable Set it to KEYCLOAK_FIRST_USER_EMAIL your email. It is your admin login for the API KEYCLOAK_FIRST_USER_PASSWORD a password you will remember. Quote it if it has special characters, because bash reads the file

Leave CLUSTER_NAME=fn, NAMESPACE=fn and RELEASE_NAME=fn-dev as they are, and leave the other lines alone. The cluster name and namespace are written into the Tiltfile, the example files and the port-forward scripts. Your own names go in your own files under bootstrap/ (later steps), not here.

In k8s/federated-node/dev.values.yaml, set nodeId to a name for your node (any text; it is required, and names the node in the results it delivers). Leave db.host as db.fn.svc, which has to match NAMESPACE, and every image tag as latest. The Gitea block is already switched on, and the chart generates its admin password.

docs.title: 4. Install fncli
docs.text:
Do this before the deploy in step 5: mise run deploy runs fncli experiment deploy.

mise trust               # if mise asks
mise run setup
fncli hello-world        # Hello, world!

mise run setup installs fncli, editable, into .venv at the repo root. With mise activated, fncli is on your PATH anywhere in the repo. The install belongs to that checkout, so a worktree needs its own mise run setup. If you installed fncli with pipx before, remove that copy: pipx uninstall phems.

Make your context file. It says which node fncli works on, and which project and way fncli trigger uses when you do not say. It is gitignored, so it stays local:

cp bootstrap/examples/context.yaml bootstrap/context.yaml

The example already matches this guide: nexus-api at http://localhost:5000, the kubectl context kind-fn, the Keycloak namespace, and .dev.env as the env file. Set defaults.project to the demo you run: demo-gitea or demo-github.

docs.title: 5. Cluster and deploy
docs.text:
mise run helm deps       # fetch the chart's subcharts (a fresh clone has none)
mise run cluster up      # a local registry, two pull-through caches, and a kind cluster called fn
mise run deploy          # build every image, install the chart (up to 10 minutes)

The first run is slow, because Docker has no cache yet. At the end mise run deploy prints the database passwords the chart generated. It runs helm upgrade --install, so it is safe to rerun for chart changes; use mise run teardown first to start from empty data. It also stops a running Tilt, so deploy first and start Tilt after.

Start Tilt in a second terminal and leave it running:

tilt up --stream

Wait until its resources are green. Once the Dagster code location has loaded, the dagster-reload resource prints the list of URLs: that is your ready signal.

What Where nexus-api http://localhost:5000 (docs at /docs) Gitea http://localhost:4000 Dagster UI http://localhost:3000 Keycloak http://localhost:8080 nexus UI http://localhost:8088/nexus-ui/ Tilt dashboard http://localhost:10350

Check that it is healthy:

kubectl config current-context        # kind-fn
kubectl get pods -n fn                # all Running, a gitea pod among them
kubectl get jobs -A                   # the *-db-init and keycloak-realm-init jobs Completed
source .dev.env
curl -sS -X POST localhost:5000/login \
  -F "username=$KEYCLOAK_FIRST_USER_EMAIL" \
  -F "password=$KEYCLOAK_FIRST_USER_PASSWORD" | jq -r .token

The login prints a token when nexus-api and Keycloak work. Do not paste it anywhere.

docs.title: 6. The demo database and the sensors
docs.text:
Both demos use one dataset, demo-db: a tiny Postgres with a cdm.person table of three rows and an empty results schema, in its own experiments release.

fncli experiment deploy                 # the release: the database, its role and secret
fncli experiment seed demo          # the schemas and rows
fncli experiment setup demo         # registers demo-db (and its secret) with the node
kubectl get pods -n experiments     # the database Running

Every Dagster sensor starts stopped, and nothing runs a merged pull request until you start them:

fncli start-sensor --group all
fncli sensor-status

If it says a sensor is not found, Dagster is still loading its code: wait a minute and run it again. After a new mise run deploy or mise run teardown, start the sensors again.

docs.title: 7. The Gitea demo
docs.text:
Everything lives in the cluster's Gitea, so nothing outside is needed. The demo is two files: the global resources (the git provider, the OAuth app secrets and the two repositories), and the project, which only assigns them and the dataset.

fncli diff  -f examples/globals-gitea.yaml          # preview: reads only
fncli apply -f examples/globals-gitea.yaml          # creates the provider, secrets and both Gitea repos
fncli apply -f examples/projects/demo-gitea.yaml    # the project and its assignments (uses demo-db)
fncli demo  -f examples/projects/demo-gitea.yaml    # the guided pull request walk

apply prints what it will change, asks, then does it. Run the diff again afterwards: it should show nothing left to change.

fncli demo creates and deletes nothing. It first checks that the node matches the project file, and stops with the rows that differ if it does not, so run the applies first. Before each step it says what the step does and shows the equivalent command. Enter runs it, s skips it, q quits. After each step it prints Open: addresses for your browser, and the objects it made. The pull request step waits up to 5 minutes for the task to run. Log in to the Gitea pages as gitea_admin. Useful options:

  • -y runs every step without asking.
  • --from N starts at step N, for example after a failed step.

Run the demo again as often as you like. fncli demo -f examples/projects/demo-gitea.yaml examples/demo-failing.json makes the task fail on purpose, to see the failure path. Without the guided checks, fncli trigger --pr --merge --watch examples/demo.json opens, merges and follows a pull request directly.

Clean up:

fncli delete -f examples/projects/demo-gitea.yaml           # the project only
fncli delete -f examples/globals-gitea.yaml --all           # also the shared repos, secrets and provider

Delete is a soft delete, and it skips anything another project still uses. The Gitea repos and OAuth apps stay in Gitea, and the next run reuses them. The dataset demo-db is not in these files, so neither delete touches it.

docs.title: 8. The GitHub demo with your own repository
docs.text:
fncli never creates or deletes GitHub repositories, tokens or Apps. You make them, and your files point at them.

  1. Create the repository on GitHub, under an account or organisation you control. It must already have a commit on its default branch (tick "Add a README"). One repository plays both roles: the trigger and the results repository.
  2. Create a GitHub App and install it on only that repository, as in Set up a project: Contents and Pull requests with read and write, webhook off. Note the App ID and the installation ID, and generate a private key.
  3. Keep the key outside the repo, for example:

mkdir -p ~/.config/phems
mv <where the browser saved it>/<app>.private-key.pem ~/.config/phems/<your-app>.private-key.pem
chmod 600 ~/.config/phems/<your-app>.private-key.pem
4. Add the two ids to .dev.env, which is the env file your context names:

GH_APP_ID=<your App ID>
GH_INSTALLATION_ID=<your installation ID>
5. Give fncli a researcher token. The demo's pull requests into the trigger repository are your own work, not the node's, so they do not use the App. Either run gh auth login, or put RESEARCHER_GIT_TOKEN=<token> in .dev.env, a personal access token that can write to the repository. 6. Copy the examples and edit the copies. Your copies under bootstrap/ are gitignored:

mkdir -p bootstrap/projects
cp bootstrap/examples/globals-github.yaml bootstrap/globals-<your-name>-github.yaml
cp bootstrap/examples/projects/demo-github.yaml bootstrap/projects/<your-name>-github.yaml
Change Where The repository address The globals file, for the trigger and the results repository, and the project file, for both: all four places, https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> The secret label The globals file: the secrets: key, and secret: under both repositories. Lowercase letters, digits, - and . only The private key path The globals file, PRIVATE_KEY: {file: ...}. ~ works watch_dir and target_dir The project file. Directories in your repository, for example mgmt/requests/ and mgmt/results/. They must not overlap, because the results pull requests go to the same repository and must not look like triggers base_branch The project file, in both places: your repository's default branch The project name The project file. Different from your Gitea project's

Leave the providers: block and the dataset demo-db as they are. 7. Diff, apply, demo, delete:

fncli diff  -f bootstrap/globals-<your-name>-github.yaml
fncli apply -f bootstrap/globals-<your-name>-github.yaml
fncli apply -f bootstrap/projects/<your-name>-github.yaml
fncli demo  -f bootstrap/projects/<your-name>-github.yaml
fncli delete -f bootstrap/projects/<your-name>-github.yaml
fncli delete -f bootstrap/globals-<your-name>-github.yaml --all

In the diff, GH_APP_ID, GH_INSTALLATION_ID and the key file must say set. The demo asks nexus-api for a token for each repository and calls GitHub with it, then opens a pull request into your repository, merges it, and later merges the results pull request, which you can watch in your repository.

Nothing is deleted in your GitHub repository, and the dataset stays.

docs.title: Teardown and starting over
docs.text:
Goal Command Remove a demo project from the node fncli delete -f its project file, then fncli delete -f its globals file with --all Remove the release and all its data, keep the cluster mise run teardown, then mise run deploy again Delete the cluster, keep the registries and their images mise run cluster down, then mise run cluster up Delete the cluster and the registries ./scripts/cluster.sh down --remove-registries Teardown, new cluster and deploy in one go mise run teardown && mise run cluster down && mise run cluster up && mise run deploy

mise run teardown wipes the node's data and releases the cluster's owner. It keeps the experiments release, so the demo database survives. After mise run teardown and mise run deploy, or the full reset above, run tilt up --stream again, then fncli start-sensor --group all, then the demo. Your .dev.env, dev.values.yaml, bootstrap/context.yaml, your files under bootstrap/ and the App's key file are untouched. After the full reset, run fncli experiment deploy again if kubectl get pods -n experiments shows nothing.

fncli experiment down removes every experiment's dataset from the node and then the release. It stops while a demo project still uses demo-db: delete that project first.

docs.title: Set Up a Project
docs.text:
This is the admin's guide to what a node needs before it can run anything: the global resources (secrets, a git provider, repositories, a dataset) and a project that uses them. Install the node first (Deploy: Core).

On a real node, set these up with the API, as this page shows. Using fncli does the same from files on a development cluster, and both create the same records.

The commands are written from the API's request models. They are a guide: the API's own reference is at /docs on your node.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Secrets, datasets, git providers, and trigger and results repositories are global: they belong to no project and are created once, by an admin. A project is then assigned the ones it uses. Each assignment holds what is per project: which directory to watch, where results go, and the enabled and revoked flags. See Architecture.

Create them in this order, because each one refers to the one before:

# What Needs Holds 1 Secret nothing A git App's credentials for each repository, and the dataset's database login. Stored in Kubernetes; the API never returns the values 2 Git provider nothing The git host: GitHub or Gitea, with its web and API addresses 3 Trigger repository provider, secret The repository whose merged pull requests become tasks 4 Results repository provider, secret The repository results are pushed to, as a branch and a pull request 5 Dataset secret A database the tasks read, and where they may write 6 Project nothing The unit of work. Created disabled 7 Assignments project, and 3, 4, 5 The trigger repository (watch_dir, base_branch), the results repository (target_dir), the dataset 8 Enable the project, start the sensors 7 Nothing runs before this

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need the admin login (the first user from the install) and the node's address.

FN=https://fn.your-institution.example.com

TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/login" \
  -F "username=admin@your-institution.example.com" \
  -F "password=<the first user's password>" | jq -r .token)

AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json")

/login takes form fields, not JSON. The token lasts 8 hours, and POST /refresh_token renews it. Creating global resources and revoking things is admin only.

docs.title: Git hosts and credentials
docs.text:
The node never stores a long-lived git token. Each repository's secret holds app credentials, and nexus-api mints a short-lived token from them each time Dagster needs one. The keys in the secret say which kind it is:

Git host Secret keys Token GitHub (a GitHub App) APP_ID, INSTALLATION_ID, PRIVATE_KEY One hour, covering the one repository Gitea (an OAuth2 application) CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, REFRESH_TOKEN One hour, refreshed from the refresh token Either, as a fallback TOKEN A static token, used as it is

GitHub and Gitea repositories can be used side by side. The repository's provider picks the API client.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
1. Create the App (your organisation's settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps, New):
  2. untick Webhook "Active";
  3. Repository permissions: Contents and Pull requests, read and write;
  4. "Only on this account", and leave the user-authorisation options off.
  5. Note the App ID, then generate a private key (a .pem file). Keep it out of git.
  6. Install the App on only the repositories the node uses. The number at the end of the installation URL is the installation ID.

GitHub OAuth Apps (user tokens) are not supported. To withdraw the node's access on GitHub, remove the repository from the App's installation, or uninstall the App: GitHub has no finer switch.

docs.title: Gitea
docs.text: Gitea is the development host. The chart can run one for you (gitea.enabled), and fncli apply creates and authorises the OAuth2 application for you: see Using fncli. The chart pins Gitea's INVALIDATE_REFRESH_TOKENS=false, which makes concurrent refreshes safe. A Gitea repository that goes unused for 30 days loses its refresh token and needs authorising again.

docs.title: 1. Secrets
docs.text:
Make one per credential. A label is the name you use for it in later calls. It also becomes part of a Kubernetes name, so use lowercase letters, digits, - and ..

# A GitHub App for a repository (here shared by the trigger and the results repository)
jq -n --rawfile key your-app.private-key.pem '{
  label: "demo-repo-creds", provider: "K8S",
  values: {APP_ID: "<app id>", INSTALLATION_ID: "<installation id>", PRIVATE_KEY: $key}
}' | curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/secrets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d @- | jq

# The dataset: the database login. The keys are USERNAME and PASSWORD
curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/secrets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "label": "demo-dataset-creds", "provider": "K8S",
  "values": {"USERNAME": "<db user>", "PASSWORD": "<db password>"}
}' | jq

To rotate a value later: PATCH $FN/global/secrets/<label> with {"values": {...}}. Rewriting a secret replaces all its values, and cached tokens from the old credentials are dropped.

docs.title: 2. Git provider
docs.text:
One per git host. Repositories on the same host share it.

PROVIDER_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/providers" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "name": "github", "type": "github",
  "uri": "https://github.com", "api_uri": "https://api.github.com"
}' | jq -r .id)

type is github or gitea. uri is the host's web address and api_uri its API base URL (for Gitea: https://<host>/api/v1).

docs.title: 3. Trigger and results repositories
docs.text:
repo_path is owner/name. secret_label is the secret from step 1. The repositories have to exist already.

TRIGGER_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/repositories/triggers" "${AUTH[@]}" -d "{
  \"provider_id\": $PROVIDER_ID,
  \"repo_path\": \"your-org/fn-triggers\",
  \"secret_label\": \"demo-repo-creds\"
}" | jq -r .id)

RESULTS_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/repositories/results" "${AUTH[@]}" -d "{
  \"provider_id\": $PROVIDER_ID,
  \"repo_path\": \"your-org/fn-results\",
  \"secret_label\": \"demo-repo-creds\"
}" | jq -r .id)

One repository can be both the trigger and the results repository. Then the project's watch_dir and target_dir must not overlap, so that the results pull requests are not mistaken for triggers.

docs.title: 4. Dataset
docs.text:
DATASET_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/datasets" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "name": "uc1_omop",
  "host": "<dataset database host>",
  "port": 5432,
  "type": "postgres",
  "secret_label": "demo-dataset-creds",
  "read_schema": "cdm",
  "write_schema": "results"
}' | jq -r .id)

Fields, types and the checks that matter are on the Datasets page. Check the dataset is reachable now, instead of when the first task fails: GET /global/datasets/$DATASET_ID/healthcheck.

Tasks can only reach the database if its address is in the chart's taskNetworkPolicy.datasetEgress (Deploy: Core).

docs.title: 5. Project
docs.text:
A new project is disabled. That is deliberate: the results repository can only be assigned while the project is disabled.

PROJECT_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/projects" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "name": "uc1-demo", "description": "First project", "enabled": false
}' | jq -r .id)

docs.title: 6. Assign the resources to the project
docs.text:
PUT assigns. The id in the URL is the global resource's id, not the assignment's. A repeat PUT replaces the project's settings for that resource.

# Dataset. The first dataset assigned becomes the project's default
curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/datasets/$DATASET_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{}' | jq

# Trigger repository: the directory to watch, and the branch merges are tracked on
curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/repositories/triggers/$TRIGGER_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "watch_dir": "specs/", "base_branch": "main"
}' | jq

# Results repository: the directory results go under, and the branch results pull requests start from and go into
curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/repositories/results/$RESULTS_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "target_dir": "results/", "base_branch": "main"
}' | jq
  • base_branch is required for both repositories. It is never guessed from the repository's default branch.
  • watch_dir must not be empty. Only a pull request that adds a .json file under it becomes a task.
  • A project has one results repository.
  • The trigger assignment's starting point is set when you assign it. Pull requests merged before that are not run, unless you ask for a backfill when enabling the project.

docs.title: 7. Check, then enable
docs.text:
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/healthcheck" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq      # can every resource be reached with its token?
curl -sS "$FN/global/healthcheck" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq                     # the whole node

A failing check (a wrong token, an unreachable database or git host) shows in the body, never as a 500, and never contains a secret value. Fix what it names, then:

curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"enabled": true}' | jq

Enabling skips pull requests that were stored while the project was off. To have them run, send {"enabled": true, "backfill": true} instead.

Finally, start the sensors. Nothing is polled until you do: see Operations. Then a researcher can ask for a task: Researcher guide.

docs.title: Add another project
docs.text:
A second project reuses the global resources: create the project, then assign the same ids.

PROJECT2_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$FN/projects" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"name": "second-project"}' | jq -r .id)

curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT2_ID/datasets/$DATASET_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{}'
curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT2_ID/repositories/triggers/$TRIGGER_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"watch_dir": "specs/", "base_branch": "main"}'
curl -sS -X PUT "$FN/projects/$PROJECT2_ID/repositories/results/$RESULTS_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"target_dir": "results-two/", "base_branch": "main"}'
curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/projects/$PROJECT2_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"enabled": true}'

A merged pull request is stored once, whatever the number of projects watching the repository, and each project whose watch_dir and base_branch match gets its own task. The project's own dataset assignment decides which dataset its tasks use.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text: The repo's MANAGEMENT.md has the same walk with more notes, and SETUP_GIT_APPS.md covers the git credentials.

docs.title: Using the API
docs.text:
This guide covers everyday interactions with the nexus-api of a Federated Node 2.x: logging in, what the routes are for, and the conventions they share. A researcher does not need the API to run a task: see the Researcher guide.

Every node serves its own interactive reference at /docs, for example https://fn.your-institution.example.com/docs, and the same description as openapi.json (also in the repo's nexus/api folder). Treat those as the source of truth for request and response bodies.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: export FN=https://fn.your-institution.example.com

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
/login takes form fields, not JSON, and returns a bearer token:

TOKEN=$(curl --silent "$FN/login" \
    -F "username=your@email.com" \
    -F "password=yourpassword" | jq -r '.token')

AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json")

Tokens are valid for 8 hours by default (the chart value token.life).

docs.title: Refresh a token
docs.text: curl --silent -X POST "$FN/refresh_token" "${AUTH[@]}"

docs.title: The routes
docs.text:
Area Routes Who Health GET /health_check, GET /ready_check No login needed Login POST /login, POST /refresh_token Anyone with an account Global resources /global/secrets, /global/providers, /global/datasets, /global/repositories/triggers, /global/repositories/results Admin to create, change and revoke Users /global/users Admin Projects /projects, /projects/<id> Admin to create Assignments /projects/<id>/datasets, .../secrets, .../repositories/triggers, .../repositories/results Admin Tasks and results /projects/<id>/tasks, /projects/<id>/results Task rights. GET /tasks (every task) is admin Sensors /dagster/sensors Admin Health checks GET .../healthcheck on the node, a project, and each resource Admin

The pattern for each kind of resource is the same: GET lists or reads, POST creates (globals), PUT assigns (to a project), PATCH changes, DELETE removes. The id in the URL of an assignment is the global resource's id, not the assignment's.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Enabled and revoked. Every resource has an enabled flag, which anyone allowed to manage it can flip, and a revoked flag, which is admin only and takes effect at once. Only a resource that is enabled and not revoked is used. See Operations.
  • Soft delete. DELETE hides the record and frees its name. A resource that projects still use gives a 409 that lists them.
  • Health checks. A failing check is reported in the response body with a status of 200, never a 500, and never contains a secret value.
  • Secrets are write-only. No call returns a secret's values or even its key names.
  • Unknown fields. Some create bodies (a dataset, for example) ignore fields they do not know, so read a record back after creating it.
  • Bad input. An invalid request body is a 400. A move a record's state does not allow is a 409.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Logins are Keycloak users. An admin creates and lists them through the API:

# Create a user. The response shows a temporary password, once.
curl -sS -X POST "$FN/global/users" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{
  "email": "researcher@your-institution.example.com",
  "firstName": "Ada",
  "lastName": "Researcher",
  "role": "Users"
}' | jq

# List users, with their roles and whether they still have to set a password
curl -sS "$FN/global/users" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

Only email is required. username defaults to the email, and role to Users. A user that already exists is a 400.

The new user changes the temporary password with PUT /global/users/reset-password and the body {"email": "...", "tempPassword": "...", "newPassword": "..."}, which needs no login.

The node's roles are realm roles in Keycloak:

Role Used for Users A basic login. Researchers do not need one in the common case: they work in git. Administrator Registers and revokes the global resources, creates users, and manages projects. Super Administrator Everything an Administrator can do, plus the wider Keycloak realm permissions. System Integrations. Dagster logs in to nexus-api as a system user.

The first admin is created at install time from firstUserSecret (Deploy: Core).

docs.title: Datasets, repositories, projects
docs.text:
These are covered where you set them up:

  • Dataset fields and checks: Datasets.
  • Switching things on and off: Operations.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task is normally created by a merged pull request, so there is no "submit" call to learn: see Researcher guide. Through the API you look at tasks and manage them (admin):

# The tasks of a project, with their status
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# One task
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# The pull request that created it
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/trigger" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# Its results delivery
curl -sS "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/results" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

# Queue a failed or canceled task for another attempt
curl -sS -X POST "$FN/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tasks/$TASK_ID/retry" "${AUTH[@]}" | jq

A task's status is PENDING, QUEUED, RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELED. The reason a task cannot start or a pull request was rejected is in state_cause.

Read a run's logs in the Dagster UI (Operations).

POST /projects/<id>/tasks creates a task without a pull request, but results delivery is built around the pull request, so such a task has no results delivery. Use a pull request.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
Nothing runs until the Dagster sensors are started. As an admin, start and stop them from the API:

# Start every sensor
curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "RUNNING"}' | jq

# Stop one
curl -sS -X PATCH "$FN/dagster/sensors/task_launcher_sensor" "${AUTH[@]}" -d '{"status": "STOPPED"}' | jq

GET /dagster/sensors lists each sensor with its status and its latest tick. See Operations.

docs.title: Using fncli
docs.text:
fncli is the command-line tool of the Federated Node repository. It sets a development node up from a few YAML files, asks the node to run a task, and checks what happened. This page explains the files and the commands.

It is a development and demo tool. Its setup commands assume the local development cluster, with Gitea as the git host and Tilt's port-forwards. On a real node, set the git provider, repositories and secrets up with the API (Set up a project). Using fncli apply or delete on a node you care about needs a decision of its own, and delete --all must never be run against one.

To install it and run the demo from nothing, see Run locally.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From the repo root, with mise installed.

mise run setup
fncli hello-world        # prints "Hello, world!"

mise run setup installs fncli, editable, into .venv at the repo root. With mise activated in your shell, fncli is on your PATH anywhere in the repo. The install belongs to that checkout, so a worktree needs its own mise run setup. If fncli fails with No module named 'fncli', or lacks a command, run mise run setup again from the checkout you want. If you installed fncli with pipx before, remove that copy: pipx uninstall phems.

fncli --help lists the commands. fncli reads cluster secrets from the current kubectl context, so check kubectl config current-context is the cluster you mean.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
Three kinds of file drive fncli. None holds a secret value, so they are safe to commit.

Path What it holds Committed bootstrap/context.yaml Which node fncli works on, and the defaults of its commands No: gitignored. bootstrap/examples/context.yaml is the example bootstrap/globals*.yaml The global resources: git providers, secrets, repositories Yes bootstrap/projects/<name>.yaml One project, and what it is assigned Yes triggers/*.json A trigger file: the task spec a pull request adds Yes experiments/<name>/dataset.yaml An experiment's dataset and its secret Yes

The files are split by who writes them and when. The node is chosen apart from the content, so the same globals and project files serve the demo, the end-to-end tests and your own node.

docs.title: The context file
docs.text:
node:
  url: http://localhost:5000          # nexus-api (the Tilt port-forward)
  kube_context: kind-fn               # fncli refuses to run when kubectl points elsewhere
  keycloak_namespace: keycloak        # where fncli's login is read from
  env_file: .dev.env                  # GH_APP_ID and friends; found from here up
defaults:
  project: demo-gitea                 # for fncli trigger and fncli demo without --project
  trigger_type: pr                    # pr, or api (not built yet)
  • Every command that talks to the node reads it. fncli looks for bootstrap/context.yaml from the current directory up, so it works from any folder of the repo. --context FILE or FNCLI_CONTEXT names another.
  • Every command refuses to run when kubectl's current context differs from node.kube_context. The context file is the one authority for the target.
  • FNCLI_DEFAULT_PROJECT and FNCLI_DEFAULT_TRIGGER_TYPE in the shell win over defaults:, and a flag wins over both. A command that uses a default says so on its first line.

docs.title: Node files
docs.text:
A node file lists any of the providers, secrets, repositories, datasets and projects of a node. The global resources go in one file and a project in another. A project file is only its name and what it is assigned, by name:

# bootstrap/examples/projects/demo-gitea.yaml
version: 1
projects:
  - name: demo-gitea
    datasets: [demo-db]                  # on the node already
    repositories:
      triggers:
        - repository: http://gitea.fn.svc:4000/gitea_admin/demo-trigger-repo
          watch_dir: specs/
          base_branch: main
      results:
        repository: http://gitea.fn.svc:4000/gitea_admin/demo-results-repo
        target_dir: results/
        base_branch: main
  • The keys are the backend's own unique fields, so a file holds no ids: provider uri, repository uri, secret label, dataset name, project name.
  • Where a value comes from. A secret's values say where fncli reads them at apply time: env, file, k8s_secret, gitea_oauth (fncli makes and authorises an OAuth app in Gitea) or generate (a random value, for stand-in credentials only). A bare string where a reference is expected is rejected, so a file can never hold a secret.
  • References across files resolve against the node. A project may name a repository, dataset or secret that is in another file, as long as it is on the node when diff reads it. One that is in neither blocks the row that names it ("not in the file or on the node"), and apply leaves that row alone.
  • -f takes a path, or one relative to the nearest bootstrap/ directory, so -f examples/globals-gitea.yaml works from anywhere in the repo.
  • Names may use only lowercase letters, digits, - and ., because they become secret labels.

docs.title: Trigger files
docs.text: A trigger file is the JSON that asks the node to run a task: {"spec": {"image": "...", "env": {...}}}. It is the same task spec a researcher adds in a pull request (Researcher guide). A path, or one relative to triggers/, works. The repo has triggers/examples/demo.json, and demo-failing.json, whose task fails on purpose.

docs.title: diff, apply, delete
docs.text:
These work in the style of kubectl.

Command What it does fncli diff -f FILE Prints one row per entity: + create, ~ change, = unchanged, ! needs a confirmation, x blocked. Changes nothing. A secret to be created lists where each value is read from and whether it can be fncli apply -f FILE [-y] [--rotate LABEL] Prints that plan, asks, then does it in dependency order: secrets, providers, Gitea repositories (if the file has a gitea: section), repositories, datasets, projects. A project is created disabled and enabled last fncli delete -f FILE [--all] [-y] Deletes the file's projects. With --all, also its repositories, datasets, secrets (with their stored values) and providers

How they behave:

  • Apply is additive. It creates and updates, and never deletes. Taking an entry out of a file changes nothing on the node.
  • Apply is repeatable. A second apply of an unchanged file changes nothing, and a failed one can be run again. It stops at the first backend error and says what was done and what was not.
  • Secrets are create-only. An existing secret is left alone. --rotate LABEL rewrites all its keys, and authorises a Gitea OAuth app again. A secret edited elsewhere is not noticed until --rotate.
  • Changes only touch what differs. An assignment that exists is changed with a PATCH of the fields that differ, so a repeated apply does not re-enable what you switched off.
  • Disruptive changes are marked. A dataset's host, port, type or schemas, and a results repository's target_dir or base_branch, are pinned into each task when it is created, so changing them fails earlier tasks. Assigning a results repository to a live project needs the project disabled, so apply asks first.
  • Delete is a soft delete through the API's DELETE routes, never with ?force=true. It works in reverse order: what uses a thing goes before the thing. What another project outside the file still uses is skipped, with the backend's reason, and delete exits 1. A provider that other repositories are on is kept.
  • Gitea repositories and OAuth apps are left in place, and fncli never creates or deletes GitHub repositories, tokens or Apps.
  • Applying a file again after delete recreates everything cleanly: a deleted name is free again. When projects share globals, delete the second project's file first, then the first with --all.

docs.title: Trigger a task
docs.text:
fncli trigger --pr --merge --watch examples/demo.json

fncli trigger FILE asks the node to run a task with a trigger file. With --pr it adds the file on a new branch, under the watch directory of the project's trigger repository, and opens a pull request (taken from the project's record in the node, not from any env). With --merge it merges the pull request, which is what the sensors pick up, and with --watch it follows the pull request, its task and its run, and exits 1 on a rejection or a failed run.

The project and the way default to the context's defaults. --api is reserved for sending the same file to the task API, and says it is not built yet. On GitHub, the pull requests into the trigger repository are the researcher's work, so they use RESEARCHER_GIT_TOKEN, or the token of gh auth login. On Gitea they use the admin login.

docs.title: demo
docs.text:
fncli demo -f PROJECT_FILE [TRIGGER] shows the pull request process on a node that apply has already set up. It creates and deletes nothing.

  1. It builds the plan diff prints for the project file. If anything would change, it stops with exit 1 and lists the rows. Nothing is applied for you.
  2. Then it checks the dataset and the git host, walks a pull request into the trigger repository, the task it becomes and the results pull request, then checks the whole project. Before each step it says what the step does, shows the equivalent fncli command, and asks.

The flow is apply the globals, apply the project, demo as often as you like, then delete. Run locally walks it.

docs.title: Sensors and checks
docs.text:
These act on the project in your context's defaults (or --project NAME), and talk only to nexus-api and Dagster. They are written for the development cluster.

Command What it does start-sensor / stop-sensor (--group G or --name N) Starts or stops Dagster sensors. Groups: ingest, evaluate, launcher, status, delivery, all. A group stops in reverse order sensor-status Every sensor's status and last three ticks project-show JSON of the project's resources, pull requests, tasks and results project-set --enabled/--revoked true\|false [--backfill] Enables, disables, revokes or restores a project resource-set KIND ..., global-set KIND ..., secret-set ... The flags on a project's use of a resource, on the resource itself, and on a secret project-healthcheck, verify-project The project's healthcheck, and a read-only report on it. Exit 1 on a failure verify-git-secret [--entity trigger\|results] Asks nexus-api for a git token for the repository and checks the git host accepts it merge-results-pr --number N Merges a results pull request, so the sync sensor records it as merged

KIND is trigger, results, dataset or secret. The --revoked options also need the keycloak-first-user secret that mise run deploy creates, so on a real node revoke through the API instead.
